name: Laxmi
definition: Laxmi is a composite portrait of an anganwadi worker in Jamkhandi taluk, Bagalkote district, navigating precarious employment, household debt and the schooling hopes of a family facing seasonal floods and drought. She embodies the pressures on women balancing care work, agricultural livelihoods and community responsibilities in the Krishna-Malaprabha belt.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Laxmi works as an anganwadi helper in a centre serving two hamlets outside Jamkhandi town, earning a monthly honorarium of around Rs 5,500 that arrives irregularly. Her day begins at six, preparing a breakfast of jowar rotti and shenga chutney before cycling four kilometres to the centre, where she weighs children, serves the midday meal of rice and sambar, and helps the main worker with immunisation records and preschool activities. Her husband Basavaraj owns three acres of black-soil land where they grow jowar, cotton and gram; hired labour and tractor costs mount to about Rs 25,000 each season. The 2023 drought cut cotton yields by half, forcing them to borrow Rs 40,000 from a Jamkhandi moneylender at three per cent monthly interest. Flood relief after the Krishna rose in 2024 paid only Rs 8,500 per hectare, far less than the actual loss. Evenings she cooks, tends the two buffaloes and repairs torn school uniforms. Her anganwadi wage barely covers groceries; the farm income is consumed by input costs, loan repayments and two children's school fees.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Laxmi lives with her husband Basavaraj, two children, her widowed mother-in-law and Basavaraj's unmarried younger brother in a tiled house near the Jamkhandi-Bilagi road. Her daughter Pavitra is fourteen and in Class 9 at the government high school in Jamkhandi; her son Sharan is eleven and in Class 6 at the same school. Laxmi was married at nineteen after completing SSLC; Basavaraj finished Class 10 but never went further. Pavitra dreams of becoming a nurse, and Laxmi insists she stay in school despite relatives suggesting she help at home or marry early. Gender roles are fixed: Laxmi cooks all meals, fetches water from the shared borewell, manages the anganwadi work and buffaloes, while Basavaraj and his brother handle field labour and trips to the APMC. Her mother-in-law, now frail, once worked as a daily-wage labourer and receives a widow pension of Rs 1,000 monthly.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Laxmi herself passed SSLC from a Kuruba hostel in Jamkhandi in 2007, the first girl in her family to complete secondary school; her parents pulled her out after tenth because they could not afford the bus fare to Bagalkote for PU. Pavitra studies in the Kannada-medium government high school where textbooks are free under the government scheme, but Laxmi pays around Rs 1,200 yearly for the uniform, notebooks and a private mathematics tutor who charges Rs 300 monthly. Sharan attends the same school and brings home midday-meal benefits; both children receive Shakti bus passes, sparing the family about Rs 400 monthly in transport costs. Laxmi dreams of sending Pavitra to the nursing college in Bagalkote after SSLC and PU, which would cost perhaps Rs 60,000 yearly for fees and hostel.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Laxmi's mother-in-law suffers from joint pain and occasional breathlessness; the nearest primary health centre is six kilometres away in Jamkhandi, and doctors refer serious cases to Bagalkote district hospital, a forty-kilometre bus ride costing Rs 150 return. Laxmi herself is anaemic—her haemoglobin was 9.8 g/dL at the last anganwadi check—and tires easily, though she rarely rests. Pavitra complains of stomach pain during exams, which Laxmi attributes to exam stress and irregular meals when money is short. The anganwadi distributes iron tablets and deworming doses, but many mothers skip follow-up visits. Laxmi worries about fluoride in the borewell water; neighbours speak of dental stains and joint problems, though no one has money for water filters. Dengue struck the hamlet in the 2024 monsoon, and one child was hospitalised in Bagalkote for a week; the family borrowed Rs 12,000 for treatment despite Ayushman Bharat coverage, because they had to pay upfront and wait for reimbursement. Health expenses deepen debt faster than any other shock.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Laxmi's family belongs to the Kuruba community, traditionally shepherds and now mostly small farmers and labourers in Bagalkote; Kurubas form a significant part of the district's population and many identify with the Kaginele Kanaka Guru Peetha. Laxmi visits the Banashankari temple in Badami once a year during the jatra, a half-day trip by bus with Pavitra and her mother-in-law, seeking blessings for the children's education and the farm's prosperity. Caste shapes social ties: Laxmi's anganwadi serves Kuruba, Lingayat and SC Holeya families, and she navigates caste sensitivities around seating and utensils diplomatically, though upper-caste parents sometimes complain. Her husband attends Kuruba community meetings in Jamkhandi where leaders discuss the demand for Scheduled Tribe status and political alignments; some support Congress, others BJP. Festivals such as Ugadi and Deepavali are marked with new clothes if money permits; Sharan participates in Huttari, the jowar harvest festival. The anganwadi also runs SHG meetings where women discuss microfinance loans, though Laxmi has not joined, fearing she cannot repay another instalment.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Laxmi receives her anganwadi honorarium through direct bank transfer, though delays of two or three months are routine, forcing her to borrow for groceries. Pavitra and Sharan hold Shakti bus passes issued in mid-2026, which save the family considerable expense; Laxmi herself uses Shakti for the rare trip to Bagalkote, marvelling that women can now travel without paying, though she hears the NWKRTC complains of unpaid dues. The family has a yellow ration card and collects ten kilograms of rice monthly under Anna Bhagya; Laxmi would prefer cash, as neighbours do, to buy jowar flour instead, but the system is rigid. Gruha Lakshmi payments began reaching her account in late 2023, Rs 2,000 monthly, but instalments have been delayed since mid-2025; she tracks the news anxiously because that money pays the tutor. Flood relief in 2024 came months late and covered only part of the cotton loss. The gram panchayat is dominated by Lingayat leaders; Kuruba voices are fewer, though the taluk panchayat member is Kuruba. Laxmi has attended one Janaspandana grievance day but got no response about the anganwadi building's leaking roof.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Laxmi worries most about keeping Pavitra in school until she finishes PU and enters nursing college; every rupee of debt and every delayed wage threatens that dream. She resents that Kalyana Karnataka districts receive Article 371(J) funds and a Kalaburagi secretariat while Bagalkote, equally poor, gets nothing beyond Belagavi's ten-day winter session, which feels like a symbolic gesture. She blames both drought and government for the farm crisis: Almatti dam's height has not been raised, Malaprabha canal water comes irregularly, and crop insurance pays a pittance. She fears Pavitra will marry early if money runs out, and that Sharan will migrate to Goa or Pune for work, leaving the farm and the old to fend for themselves.
